L10: # Model Training with Ultralytics YOLO【5†#】
L11: 
L12: 【6†Image: Ultralytics YOLO ecosystem and integrations†cdn.ul.run】
L13: ## Introduction【7†#】
L14: Training a 【8†deep learning†www.ultralytics.com】 model involves feeding it data and adjusting its parameters so that it can make accurate predictions. Train mode in Ultralytics YOLO26 is engineered for effective and efficient training of object detection models, fully utilizing modern hardware capabilities. This guide aims to cover all the details you need to get started with training your own models using YOLO26's robust set of features.
L15: If you haven't installed Ultralytics yet, start with the 【9†Quickstart guide】.
L16: See the 【10†unreleased YOLO27 preview】 for planned training examples.
L17: 
L18: 【11†YouTube video player†www.youtube-nocookie.com】
L19: Watch: How to Train a YOLO model on Your Custom Dataset in Google Colab.
L20: ## Why Choose Ultralytics YOLO for Training?【12†#】
L21: 
L22: Here are some compelling reasons to opt for YOLO26's Train mode:
L23:   * Efficiency: Make the most out of your hardware, whether you're on a single-GPU setup or scaling across multiple GPUs.
L24:   * Versatility: Train on custom datasets in addition to readily available ones like COCO, VOC, and ImageNet.
L25:   * User-Friendly: Simple yet powerful CLI and Python interfaces for a straightforward training experience.
L26:   * Hyperparameter Flexibility: A broad range of customizable hyperparameters to fine-tune model performance. For deeper control, you can 【13†customize the trainer】 itself.
L27:   * Cloud Training: Train on cloud GPUs through 【14†Ultralytics Platform】 with real-time metrics and automatic checkpointing.
L28: ### Key Features of Train Mode【15†#】
L29: 
L30: The following are some notable features of YOLO26's Train mode:
L31:   * Automatic Dataset Download: Dataset configurations with a download source are downloaded automatically on first use, e.g., `yolo train data=coco8.yaml`. See the 【16†Datasets overview】 for supported formats and datasets.
L32:   * Multi-GPU Support: Scale your training efforts seamlessly across multiple GPUs to expedite the process.
L33:   * Hyperparameter Configuration: The option to modify hyperparameters through YAML configuration files or CLI arguments.
L34:   * Visualization and Monitoring: Real-time tracking of training metrics and visualization of the learning process for better insights.
L35: ## Usage Examples【17†#】
L36: 
L37: Train YOLO26n on the COCO8 dataset for 100 【18†epochs†www.ultralytics.com】 at image size 640. The training device can be specified using the `device` argument. If no argument is passed, GPU `device=0` will be used when available; otherwise `device='cpu'` will be used. See the Arguments section below for a full list of training arguments.
L38: 
L39: Windows Multi-Processing Error
L40: On Windows, you may receive a `RuntimeError` when launching the training as a script. Add an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block before your training code to resolve it.
L41: 
L42: Single-GPU and CPU Training Example
L43: 
L44: Device is determined automatically. If a GPU is available, it will be used (default CUDA device 0); otherwise training will start on CPU.
L45: [Button: Python][Button: CLI]
L46: 
L47:     `from ultralytics import YOLO
L48: 
L49:     # Load a model
L50:     model = YOLO("yolo26n.yaml")  # build a new model from YAML
L51:     model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")  # load a pretrained model (recommended for training)
L52:     model = YOLO("yolo26n.yaml").load("yolo26n.pt")  # build from YAML and transfer weights
L53: 
L54:     # Train the model
L55:     results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640)`
L56: ### Multi-GPU Training【19†#】
L57: 
L58: Multi-GPU training allows for more efficient utilization of available hardware resources by distributing the training load across multiple GPUs. This feature is available through both the Python API and the command-line interface. To enable multi-GPU training, specify the GPU device IDs you wish to use.
L59: 
L60: Multi-GPU Training Example
L61: 
L62: To train with 2 GPUs, CUDA devices 0 and 1 use the following commands. Expand to additional GPUs as required.
L63: [Button: Python][Button: CLI]
L64: 
L65:     `from ultralytics import YOLO
L66: 
L67:     # Load a model
L68:     model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")  # load a pretrained model (recommended for training)
L69: 
L70:     # Train the model with 2 GPUs
L71:     results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, device=[0, 1])
L72: 
L73:     # Train the model with the two most idle GPUs
L74:     results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, device=[-1, -1])`
L75: 
L76: Windows Multi-GPU Support
L77: Multi-GPU training does not work on Windows with the official PyTorch wheels for `torch>=2.4`. Ultralytics launches DDP through `torch.distributed.run`, whose rendezvous step builds a `TCPStore` that has defaulted to the libuv backend since PyTorch 2.4, and the official Windows wheels are built without libuv. Training exits immediately with:
L78: 
L79: `RuntimeError: use_libuv was requested but PyTorch was built without libuv support `
L80: Setting `USE_LIBUV=0` does not resolve this, because the rendezvous constructs the `TCPStore` directly and that code path never reads the variable. Train on Linux or 【20†WSL2†learn.microsoft.com】 to use multiple GPUs, or train on a single GPU with `device=0` on Windows.
L81: 
L82: Multi-GPU Training with Custom Code
L83: When you specify multiple devices (e.g., `device=[0, 1]`), Ultralytics internally spawns a new trainer instance and executes `torch.distributed.run` under the hood. This works seamlessly for standard CLI usage and unmodified Python scripts.
L84: However, if your script contains custom components—such as a custom trainer, validator, dataset, or augmentation pipeline—these objects cannot be automatically serialized and transferred to the DDP subprocesses. In this case, you must launch your script directly with `torch.distributed.run`:
L85: 
L86:     `python -m torch.distributed.run --nproc_per_node 2 your_training_script.py`
L87: AMD GPU training uses a PyTorch ROCm build with the standard `device=0` or `device=cuda:0` syntax. See the 【21†AMD integration guide】 for ROCm installation, multi-GPU training, AMP notes, and 【22†MIGraphX inference】 of exported models.
L88: 
L89: Intel GPU training uses `device=xpu:0`, or multiple XPU IDs with a PyTorch build that provides XCCL.
L90: ### Huawei Ascend NPU Training【23†#】
L91: 
L92: Ultralytics supports training and validation on Huawei Ascend NPUs through 【24†`torch_npu`†github.com】. Install mutually compatible CANN, PyTorch, and `torch_npu` versions by following the 【25†Ascend Extension for PyTorch installation guide†github.com】, then source the CANN environment before starting Ultralytics:
L93: 
L94:     `source /usr/local/Ascend/ascend-toolkit/set_env.sh`
L95: 
L96: Ascend NPU Training Example
L97: [Button: Python][Button: CLI]
L98: 
L99:     `from ultralytics import YOLO
L100: 
L101:     model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
L102: 
L103:     # Train on one Ascend NPU
L104:     results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, device="npu:0")
L105: 
L106:     # Train across two Ascend NPUs with HCCL
L107:     results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, device="npu:0,1")`
L108: The standard training features, including AMP, validation, checkpointing, and resume, use the active NPU. AutoBatch is available for single-NPU training, while multiple NPU IDs launch distributed training through HCCL. See the 【26†Huawei Ascend integration guide】 for model export and deployment after training.
L109: ### Idle GPU Training【27†#】
L110: 
L111: Idle GPU Training enables automatic selection of the least utilized GPUs in multi-GPU systems, optimizing resource usage without manual GPU selection. This feature identifies available GPUs based on utilization metrics and VRAM availability.
L112: 
L113: Idle GPU Training Example
L114: 
L115: To automatically select and use the most idle GPU(s) for training, use the `-1` device parameter. This is particularly useful in shared computing environments or servers with multiple users.
L116: [Button: Python][Button: CLI]
L117: 
L118:     `from ultralytics import YOLO
L119: 
L120:     # Load a model
L121:     model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")  # load a pretrained model (recommended for training)
L122: 
L123:     # Train using the single most idle GPU
L124:     results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, device=-1)
L125: 
L126:     # Train using the two most idle GPUs
L127:     results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, device=[-1, -1])`
L128: 
L129: The auto-selection algorithm prioritizes GPUs with:
L130:   1. Lower current utilization percentages
L131:   2. Higher available memory (free VRAM)
L132: 
L133: This feature is especially valuable in shared computing environments or when running multiple training jobs across different models. It automatically adapts to changing system conditions, ensuring optimal resource allocation without manual intervention.
L134: ### Apple Silicon MPS Training【28†#】
L135: 
L136: With the support for Apple silicon chips integrated in the Ultralytics YOLO models, it's now possible to train your models on devices utilizing the powerful Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) framework. The MPS offers a high-performance way of executing computation and image processing tasks on Apple's custom silicon.
L137: To enable training on Apple silicon chips, you should specify 'mps' as your device when initiating the training process. Below is an example of how you could do this in Python and via the command line:
L138: 
L139: MPS Training Example
L140: [Button: Python][Button: CLI]
L141: 
L142:     `from ultralytics import YOLO
L143: 
L144:     # Load a model
L145:     model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")  # load a pretrained model (recommended for training)
L146: 
L147:     # Train the model with MPS
L148:     results = model.train(data="coco8.yaml", epochs=100, imgsz=640, device="mps")`
L149: While leveraging the computational power of the Apple silicon chips, this enables more efficient processing of the training tasks. For more detailed guidance and advanced configuration options, please refer to the 【29†PyTorch MPS documentation†docs.pytorch.org】.
L150: ### Resuming Interrupted Trainings【30†#】
L151: 
L152: Resuming training from a previously saved state is a crucial feature when working with deep learning models. This can come in handy in various scenarios, like when the training process has been unexpectedly interrupted, or when you wish to continue training a model with new data or for more epochs.
L153: When training is resumed, Ultralytics YOLO loads the weights from the last saved model and also restores the optimizer state, 【31†learning rate†www.ultralytics.com】 scheduler, epoch number, and dataset. This allows you to continue the training process seamlessly from where it was left off. Pass an explicit `data=` alongside `resume` to continue on a different dataset instead of the checkpoint's.
L154: You can easily resume training in Ultralytics YOLO by setting the `resume` argument to `True` when calling the `train` method, and specifying the path to the `.pt` file containing the partially trained model weights.
L155: 
L156: Below is an example of how to resume an interrupted training using Python and via the command line:
L157: 
L158: Resume Training Example
L159: [Button: Python][Button: CLI]
L160: 
L161:     `from ultralytics import YOLO
L162: 
L163:     # Load a model
L164:     model = YOLO("path/to/last.pt")  # load a partially trained model
L165: 
L166:     # Resume training
L167:     results = model.train(resume=True)`
L168: 
L169: By setting `resume=True`, the `train` function will continue training from where it left off, using the state stored in the 'path/to/last.pt' file. If the `resume` argument is omitted or set to `False`, the `train` function will start a new training session.
L170: Remember that checkpoints are saved at the end of every epoch by default, or at fixed intervals using the `save_period` argument, so you must complete at least 1 epoch to resume a training run.
L171: ## Train Settings【32†#】
L172: The training settings for YOLO models encompass various hyperparameters and configurations used during the training process. These settings influence the model's performance, speed, and 【33†accuracy†www.ultralytics.com】. Key training settings include batch size, learning rate, momentum, and weight decay. Additionally, the choice of optimizer, 【34†loss function†www.ultralytics.com】, and training dataset composition can impact the training process.
L173: Careful tuning and experimentation with these settings are crucial for optimizing performance.
L174: ### MuSGD Optimizer【35†#】
L175: 
L176: In YOLO26, MuSGD is a hybrid optimizer that combines standard SGD updates with Muon-style orthogonalized updates.
L177: 
L178: It is recommended for longer YOLO26 training runs and larger datasets, where orthogonalized Muon updates can help stabilize optimization.
L179: 
L180: Only 2D linear weights and 4D convolutional filters (reshaped to 2D) receive the Muon style update together with SGD, while all other parameters, such as batch normalization weights and bias terms, remain on standard SGD.
L181: When `optimizer=auto` is used, Ultralytics automatically selects MuSGD for longer training runs (typically when iterations > 10000). For shorter runs, the trainer falls back to AdamW. In `auto` mode, the trainer also selects the learning rate, so a user-provided `lr0` is ignored. To control these settings manually, select an optimizer explicitly, for example `optimizer=AdamW lr0=0.001`.
L182: 
L183: Example usage:
L184: 
L185:     `yolo train model=yolo26n.pt data=coco8.yaml optimizer=MuSGD`
L186: See the implementation in `ultralytics/optim/muon.py` and the optimizer auto-selection logic in `BaseTrainer.build_optimizer`.
L187: Argument  | Type  | Default  | Description
L188: --- | --- | --- | ---
L189: `model`  | `str`  | `None`  | Specifies the model file for training. Accepts a path to either a `.pt` pretrained model or a `.yaml` configuration file. Essential for defining the model structure or initializing weights.
L190: `data`  | `str`  | `None`  | Path to the dataset YAML (e.g., `coco8.yaml`), which carries the paths to training and 【36†validation data†www.ultralytics.com】, class names, and number of classes. Classification instead takes a dataset directory or a built-in dataset name (e.g., `imagenet10`).
L191: `epochs`  | `int`  | `100`  | Total number of training epochs. Each 【18†epoch†www.ultralytics.com】 represents a full pass over the entire dataset. Adjusting this value can affect training duration and model performance.
L192: `time`  | `float`  | `None`  | Maximum training time in hours. If set, this overrides the `epochs` argument, allowing training to automatically stop after the specified duration. Useful for time-constrained training scenarios.
